name: FOMO in QC Investment
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Rush to Not Be Left Behind
lesson.summary: This section explains how FOMO distorts quantum computing investment decisions, showing why fear of a competitor's advantage can override careful cost-benefit reasoning.
lesson.body:
You already know that cognitive biases work by substituting an easy mental shortcut for a harder, more effortful judgment. FOMO in quantum computing investment is a specific case of that substitution: instead of asking "will this technology deliver a return within our planning horizon?", a decision-maker asks the much easier question "what are our competitors doing?" and then matches it. The hard question requires forecasting an uncertain technology timeline, estimating a probability of payoff, and weighing that against the opportunity cost of the money elsewhere ,  real analytical work with no guaranteed answer. The easy question just requires watching what peer organizations announce and reacting to it.

The reason this substitution feels rational in the moment rather than reckless is that it taps into loss aversion, a pattern where the pain of a potential loss looms larger than the pleasure of an equivalent gain. Losing competitive ground to a rival who invested early feels like a concrete, personal failure that a decision-maker will be blamed for later. Missing out on a return by investing too early and getting little back feels like a diffuse, industry-wide risk that everyone can plausibly claim was unforeseeable. Because the two outcomes are treated so asymmetrically, spending money defensively ,  just in case a rival gets ahead ,  starts to look like the "safe" choice, even though it is really just a different, harder-to-quantify gamble.

This is worsened by the fact that quantum computing's payoff timeline is genuinely uncertain, which is exactly the condition under which people lean hardest on social cues instead of independent analysis. When nobody can confidently calculate an expected return, watching what respected peers or competitors do becomes a stand-in for evidence ,  a pattern sometimes called social proof. If several large companies in an industry announce quantum initiatives, each additional announcement makes the technology look more validated, which makes the next organization's decision to invest feel less like speculation and more like simply keeping pace with an emerging standard, even if none of the underlying uncertainty about near-term returns has actually changed.

Picture a technology executive who has to decide whether to commit a multi-year budget to a quantum computing pilot. A rigorous analysis would ask what problem the organization is trying to solve, whether current quantum hardware can plausibly solve it better than classical alternatives within the budget period, and what else that money could accomplish. Under FOMO, that analysis gets short-circuited: the executive instead reasons that two direct competitors have already launched quantum programs, and being the one company without one carries a visible reputational risk if quantum computing turns out to matter later. The commitment gets approved primarily to avoid that visible risk, not because the cost-benefit case was worked through ,  which means the organization has effectively let competitors' choices, rather than its own analysis, set its budget.
